lignes.texte: If you overdose on a drug, an ER can pump your stomach.
Take too much of a weight loss shot and it’s a different, terrifying reality.
GLP-1 medicines like Ozempic and Wegovy bypass your digestive system completely.
There’s no flushing it out. There’s no antidote.
Just one slight miscalculation in dosing triggered a 72 hour metabolic emergency.
And medical science has no way to turn it off.
7 AM
Your alarm goes off. It’s time to take your GLP-1,
but this week, the syringe looks a little different.
You recently switched to an online telehealth company. So your new doctor
sent a compounded version of Wegovy. Thanks to surging popularity, there’s
a nationwide shortage of GLP-1 medications. So the brand names are becoming harder to find.
But this looks different from your usual pre-filled, single dose pen. This compound
version has multiple doses in a vial. And it's measured in units instead of
the milliliters you’re normally used to. The conversion is confusing. The telehealth
instructions were sent by automated email. You have absolutely no one to ask for help.
Using the tiny syringe, you draw out what you think is your usual 5 units.
Except you just made a mistake.
You’re out by a single decimal point Instead of 0.05 milliliters, you’re about to inject 0.50.
50 units.
Ten times your normal dose. Shockingly, this is the most common dosing
error for GLP-1 medications. A full 68% of overdoses happen because of this confusion.
The chemical effect on your body is massive.
It’s like accidentally drinking 10 shots of espresso when you
only intended to take a sip of decaf. The rise of telehealth, compounded alternatives,
medical spas, and the lack of standardization in units across different brands have created
a ticking health bomb for GLP-1 medication users. It’s why dosing and therapeutic errors account for
91% of overdose cases reported to poison control centers.
Obesity medicine physician Dr. Leslie Golden agrees, stating:
“many of these ‘overdose’ stories are… about fragmented care, inadequate education, inaccurate
information from influencers and desperation for treatment rather than the medication itself.”
There are other overdose causes: first-time patients who believe their medication requires a
daily dose instead of a weekly dose. Or long-time patients who miss a week and think the best way to
fix it is by doubling up their next dose. 8 AM
Thanks to your misdosing, you’re staring down a scary situation.
Turns out, your provider made a mistake in the conversion.
But it’s too late. It’s already in your system.
9 AM For the first few hours, you go about your
day normally. You make it into the office, sit down at your desk and start the day’s meetings.
Nothing is off. Nothing seems out of the ordinary. But beneath the surface,
a biological nightmare is unfolding.
The massive dose of semaglutide is entering your bloodstream. It’s coursing through you,
reaching your brain, hijacking your nervous system and tricking your body into thinking you’re full.
You’re a ticking time bomb… you just don’t know it yet.
11 AM
You get a strange rumble in your stomach. Maybe it was
something you ate at breakfast or too much coffee.
It’s not.
You’re experiencing the first symptom 94% of
patients with GLP-1 medication overdoses experience: nausea.
You try to ignore the symptoms. If you can just make it through
your lunch break, you can get to a pharmacy.
1 PM
You buy an over-the-counter antiemetic called meclizine
hoping it’ll do the trick so you can get back to work.
It’s pointless.
Nausea caused by a semaglutide overdose doesn’t respond well to over-the-counter
treatments. That’s because it’s coming from your brain. Meclizine,
and other drugs like it, are completely useless.
You go back to your desk and try to ignore the increasing wave of
nausea flooding over you. You skip lunch, your appetite completely shot.
2 PM
The first major incident hits.
You’re sitting in a conference room when a hot flash prickles across your face and
your heart rate spikes. It feels like your heart is thumping right out of your chest.
A vice like tightness briefly grips you. A cold sweat breaks out across your forehead.
Your stomach grumbles audibly. Your co-workers
cast worried and disgusted glances at you. But no one says anything.
You excuse yourself mid-sentence, hurriedly leave the room and sprint down the hall. You
burst through the communal toilet door, into a stall and start dry heaving. The next 10 minutes
are spent gripping the cold porcelain of the toilet retching, terrified someone will hear you.
Eventually it stops. You splash cold water over your face,
pat a paper towel on your skin and sheepishly go back to the conference room.
6 PM
You endure the commute from hell,
every bump jolts your stomach. You feel like you could throw up any second.
The 12 hour mark is approaching and your body is hitting its absolute limit.
You make it home and collapse on the couch. You skip dinner. You feel drained, dizzy and sluggish.
8 PM
You’re lying flat on the couch, trying to ride it out and watch television.
Suddenly, you feel a sharp, metallic taste at the back of your throat.
Your saliva starts flowing rapidly.
You’re about to vomit.
You run to the bathroom, barely making it to the toilet before violently hurling the
contents of your stomach into the bowl. You feel dazed as you wipe the drool from your mouth.
It’s not the first time you’ve had nausea as a side effect of the GLP-1s. It’s one of the most
common reactions. 8.30 PM
Just 30 minutes later, the exact same feeling comes up. You run back to the
bathroom and in between heaves, start to worry about what’s happening to you.
You projectile vomit, barely making the target.
The next hour is spent crouched on the floor, sweaty and panicking.
Like most semaglutide overdoses, vomiting starts within 12 to 24 hours of receiving the incorrect
dose. But this isn’t just any nausea and vomiting. You’re experiencing something far more intense,
something other patients have described as “the worst nausea I’ve ever had”.
Unlike a simple stomach bug, the vomiting caused by GLP-1 medication overdoses
is so severe it’s almost always projectile. And it’s so frequent,
patients report it can happen 8-12 times in a single 24-hour period.
Medically, this is known as hyperemesis.
9 PM
Deep inside the brainstem is the Area Postrema. This is the part of the body
that controls the vomiting reflex. And right now, it’s being swamped by semaglutide.
The overdose is so intense, your biological “panic
button” has broken. It’s now stuck in the “ON” position.
And it gets worse.
The overdose is amplifying the core effect of your medication: delayed gastric emptying.
Normally, semaglutide slows down digestion, helping you to feel full.
But a 10 fold dose paralyzes the system. Gastric emptying can slow by over 50% during a GLP-1
overdose. This backs up the gastrointestinal system and causes severe pain and distress.
Your high-speed digestive highway instantly turns into a 72-hour gridlock.
12 AM
You barely get any sleep that night as your stomach violently
churns. You’ve never felt anything like it.
Day 2: 6 AM
You lie on your bed, the sheets soaked with sweat as your stomach continues to
rumble. You stagger to the bathroom, vomit one more time. That’s when you see it.
Blood.
Frantic and scared, you get yourself to the emergency room immediately.
The entire time, you’re battling nausea and asking to stop the car so you can
throw up. But eventually, you’re at the emergency room. Your ordeal is almost over.
Or is it?
9 AM
Your name is called and you stumble to the exam room.
Suddenly, a dizzy spell hits you. Your vision blurs and you almost pass out. You
catch yourself just in time and sit down with the doctor. His questions
are surprisingly hard to understand. Your mind feels cloudy and confused.
These are the signs of the second big symptom of GLP-1 overdoses: dehydration.
It usually strikes about 24 to 48 hours after the dose.
You quickly tell the doctors what’s been happening to her since you took the GLP-1
dose. Based on the symptoms, he tells you that it sounds like an overdose.
An overdose? On a GLP-1? It’s not something you got off the street. The doctor explains
that we’re capable of overdosing on almost every drug. Including Ozempic and Wegovy
You have a hard time to believe it’s that serious.
The doctor, on the other hand, takes one look at you and says he needs to admit
you. At least overnight. Exhausted and confused,
you try to find another solution. You throw an obvious suggestion: “If it’s an overdose,
you can pump my stomach, right?” The doctor shakes his head. GLP-1s
don’t work like that. There is no antidote. There’s no way to quickly
remove the medication from your body. The GLP-1 is already in your subcutaneous tissue.
It’s going to stay there.
For a while.
Semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist. Once it finds its way into your body,
it binds to GLP-1 receptors and remains active for days. Unlike other overdoses,
there’s no GLP-1 receptor antagonist to block it. There’s no chemical off switch.
You panic and ask what the doctors can do.
The honest answer?
Not much.
All they can do is manage your systems and keep you hydrated. That means IV fluids,
electrolyte monitoring and replacement, and anti-nausea medication.
But vomiting and dehydration are only the beginning.
Your body is about to be wracked by the semaglutide running through
it. And you have no way to stop the surge.
12 PM
You’re admitted to the hospital for monitoring. You still can’t stop vomiting. All that stress
on your body is causing it to physically ache. Just like all the other patients suffering the
ordeal. Leslie Gammon, another accidental overdose case, said “my ribs felt like they were being
beaten up”. 2 PM
Doctors have hooked you up to an IV. It’s a welcome relief, your mouth is completely dry.
Every time you even try to drink water, it comes back up. You’re running dangerously low on fluids;
woozy, dazed, with a total lack of energy. Dehydration has a number
of hidden dangers. It’s not just a matter of you feeling thirsty,
your doctors are beginning to whisper about kidney damage.
Horrified at the thought of yet another symptom showing up,
you ask what that means. The doctors tell you that your kidneys would struggle to filter the
waste in your blood. That means toxic waste can build up, disrupting the blood’s chemical makeup.
In severe cases, it’s fatal. The doctors ask what other medications
you’re taking. Barely able to understand what’s happening anymore due to sheer exhaustion and
confusion from the dehydration, you ask why they want to know. They say that if you’re
taking diuretics or blood pressure drugs, the risk to your kidneys is more severe. But if not,
there’s less of a chance of kidney injury. At least it’s some slightly positive news.
All you take is insulin for your diabetes. The doctor’s face stays serious. Insulin, combined
with your GLP-1 overdose, puts you at risk for a massive blood sugar drop. They’ll have to monitor
her for hypoglycemia as well. It’s best if you stay in the hospital for a couple more days.
While hypoglycemia only develops in 7% of non-diabetic patients,
it develops in 43% of diabetic patients. That’s almost a one in two chance.
What will hypoglycemia feel like?
Sweating. Tremors. Confusion. You hear the symptoms, and wonder how you’re supposed
to differentiate them from the sweating and confusion you're already feeling.
The doctors leave. You’re still throwing up, but a little less frequently now.
The prescription anti-nausea medication the doctors gave you late last night must be working.
Maybe the symptoms are starting to go away? It’s a glimmer of hope…
One that’s about to be shattered.
9 PM
You suddenly feel a pain ebbing up in your stomach. You’ve been cramping
already because of the hyperemesis and empty stomach. But this pain is new.
And getting worse. You frantically smash
the nurse call button. When help arrives, you’re doubled over in pain,
gasping for breath. The nurse immediately pumps heavy pain medication into your IV line.
When the doctor sees you, his face is etched with concern. This new abdominal
pain is different. It might complicate things. But first they have some questions.
Specifically about the dose you took. They looked it up in the system, and it’s not FDA
approved. It’s a grey market compound alternative. They have no way to understand how toxic it is.
Sarah explains that instead of her regular Wegovy, she was given a compounded alternative.
These unapproved alternatives have become increasingly popular,
making up around 35% of all US semaglutide use.
It’s a massive risk driven by desperation.
One month of Wegovy costs around $1,300 if it’s not covered by insurance. But a
compounded alternative can be found for just $250 per month. For anyone on a fixed salary,
it can be the difference between staying afloat and going into credit card debt.
But that cheap alternative just turned your body into a medical experiment.
Drug compounding is the process of mixing multiple drugs, or altering a drug. And right now,
the compounded GLP-1 market is a free for all. In fact, many compounded GLP-1s don’t even contain
the same active ingredient as the brand name they’re supposed to imitate. Others may have
the same ingredient, but in a different form. While Wegovy and Ozempic use the base form of
semaglutide, some compounders use the salt form. It might not sound like a big deal to most people.
But it creates a big risk for users.
According to the FDA, salt forms “including semaglutide sodium and semaglutide acetate,
are different active ingredients than are used in the approved drugs.” Which is why the FDA does not
approve them. 11 PM
The doctors say they can’t really know what was in the compounded GLP-1 you took. But they’re
confident that if they keep monitoring your condition, you’ll soon ride it out.
How soon? The doctors pause; at least a week. The half-life of semaglutide like Wegovy is
about 7 days. Assuming the compounded version you took is similar enough to that, the drug will be
coursing through your body for a while. That doesn’t mean the drug will be out of
your system after a week. 50% of the toxic dose will still be active. But hopefully,
the drug level should be low enough that the more severe symptoms cease.
Hopefully. In the meantime,
things will only get worse before they get better.
Because you’re about to hit the hardest peak yet.
Day 3 7 AM
As you approach the 72-hour mark, things start to nosedive.
This is the danger zone. This is the window when the GLP-1 dose peaks in your bloodstream,
between 48 and 72 hours. You haven't been able to fully sleep in days. Your
abdominal pain is only being managed by an aggressive pain medication.
But it feels like it's steadily getting worse.
Even though you already feel dizzy, weak and confused, you’re developing
new symptoms. You’ve been sweating for hours. Uncontrollably. Your heart is racing.
Suddenly, your body starts to shake.
The 48-72 hour peak window is also when overdose
patients are most at risk of developing hypoglycemia.
Nurses rush in, in response to your symptoms. Due to your already weakened condition,
they don’t want to take any chances. They immediately give you emergency
glucagon to treat the hypoglycemia, usually reserved only for the most severe cases.
Your blood sugar gets under control, but the semaglutide is still running
rampant through your gastrointestinal system. Your blood. Severely testing your kidneys.
And one more organ…
One that’s about to give out.
10 AM
As your pain medication begins to wear off,
the pain in your stomach suddenly shoots through you again.
This time, it’s unbearable. You know something is wrong. Very wrong
The pain is radiating to your back and shoulders. It’s so intense,
you can’t even pinpoint where it’s coming from. You put a hand on your stomach to try
to soothe it. But now, your skin feels tender to the touch. You start sweating
again. You’re burning up. Is the hypoglycemia back?
No. You’re one of the rare, but increasing number of people experiencing one of the
most severe possible side effects of GLP-1 overdoses:
Acute pancreatitis.
And it can be fatal.
One agency found that over a period of 18 years,
it had received reports of almost 1,300 cases of pancreatitis in people taking GLP-1s.
19 of them died Even with less severe symptoms,
thousands of Americans, and tens of thousands of people all across the world are finding themselves
in your position. Mostly through no fault of their own, as the overdose is almost always accidental.
GLP-1s have been sending countless people to the emergency room because of suspected overdoses.
You’re part of a silent, massive national – and international – epidemic.
Many people unfortunately underestimate the risk of overdosing. Under normal circumstances,
semaglutide has what experts call a “wide therapeutic window”. That
means it takes a massive amount to tip your body over the edge.
Usually you have to take at least 5 to 10 times the recommended dose.
But dangerously multiplying your dose is much easier than most people think. Particularly when
using compounded semaglutide. One 2025 study found that 4.3% of first time users “reported at least
one suspected dosing error in the first 90 days.” Some cases are even worse.
The FDA found cases where a compounded alternative,
coupled with incorrect measurement conversions,
resulted in people administering a GLP-1 dose 20 times higher than their intended dose.
From 2019 to 2023, poison control centers tracked a 1,500% increase in calls due to
GLP-1 overdoses. It’s a massive spike that mirrors the worst affected areas of the opioid epidemic.
It’s an emergency crisis that has suddenly appeared out of thin air.
And unless every GLP-1 user becomes an expert in dosing and conversions overnight, the problem is
only going to get worse. GLP-1 medication use is skyrocketing across the country. In 2024,
only 3% of U.S. adults were taking any kind of GLP-1 medication for weight loss. By 2026,
that number was up to 11%. It’s almost a fourfold increase in just 2 years.
Even if you use the correct dose, on time, every time,
the rising cost and scarce availability are forcing people to choose compounded versions.
Versions that aren’t as safe or controlled.
It’s not a user-based problem. It’s a systemic one. Obesity specialist, Dr.
Ivania Rizo wants to replace the word “overdose” with “medication or dosing error”, when it comes
to GLP-1s. Overdose implies an act of self-harm. It gives the patient a measure of intention.
But Dr. Rizo thinks the shortages, high costs, and hands-off medicine forcing people into
overdose situations should be held accountable for their role in this epidemic instead. As she says,
“the distinction matters… it shifts the focus away from blaming patients and towards the
underlying issues of product design, labeling and patient education.”
You never intended to do anything more than take your weekly prescribed medication. But now,
you’re in excruciating pain and absolutely exhausted in
a hospital bed. And your about to face your hardest day yet.
Day 4
You now have full-blown acute pancreatitis. After already experiencing hyperemesis,
moderate dehydration, and hypoglycemia, your body is in complete shock.
The doctors transfer you to the ICU to monitor your deteriorating condition. But once again,
there’s not much more they can do besides giving IV fluids and managing the pain.
At least in the ICU, they can respond to your stats and needs immediately.
One patient in your condition ended up in the ICU for 5 days as
a result of semaglutide-caused acute pancreatitis.
You’re a little luckier. In a couple of days,
your symptoms ease up. The pain lessens. The vomiting has almost entirely stopped.
Day 7
You’re discharged from the hospital entirely.
The week from hell is over. But you’re by no means back to normal. Your gastrointestinal system has
been severely compromised. Half the toxic GLP-1 dose is still floating around your system.
Will your digestive system ever fully turn back on and function like it used
to? Or have you permanently destroyed your stomach’s ability to process food?
Reports from other patients aren’t always promising. Leslie Gammon,
who underwent a similar ordeal, told NBC, “I couldn’t talk [for] nearly a week after.”
She also couldn’t keep solid food down for at least a month after her accidental overdose.
The experience scared her so much that she never returned to GLP-1s. The good news is,
since you dodged the most severe potential side effects - including kidney injury and
acute pancreatitis - you have escaped the possibility of permanent damage.
Your body takes some time to fully recuperate. You need another week of bedrest. By the end,
you’re eating plain, solid foods again.
It takes a month for your appetite to get back to more.
But the entire horrific experience has been traumatic… and expensive. The pain
you went through, and the medical bills you owe, are a reminder. One your new,
in-person physician insists on as well. From here on out, it’ll be approved GLP-1 medication only.
GLP-1’s are being touted as a miracle drug. But the truth behind it is darker than anyone wants
to admit. Watch “The Ozempic miracle. A lifelong NIGHTMARE” to find out why. Or click on this.
